title: Can you override a static method in Java?
summary: A language-specific trap question that tests whether you understand dispatch, not memorized trivia. The one-word answer is wrong without the mechanism behind it.

slides.markdown:
This question is a trap because "no" alone is the wrong answer, and "yes" alone is also the wrong answer — the code compiles and runs either way, so the interviewer is really checking whether you understand *why* it doesn't do what a naive reading suggests.

The real test is whether you can explain static (compile-time) dispatch versus dynamic (runtime) dispatch, using the exact keyword the language uses: **hiding**, not overriding.

Ask: **"Are we talking Java specifically, or object-oriented languages in general?"** This is a genuinely language-specific question — Java and C# draw a hard line between static and instance dispatch, but Python and JavaScript don't have the same static-method concept at all, so the answer doesn't port cleanly.

Asking this signals you know the behavior isn't a universal OOP law — it's a rule enforced by a particular type system.

slides.sectionTitle: The answer skeleton: no, it's hidden not overridden
slides.markdown:
Lead with: **"No — a subclass can *hide* a static method with the same signature, but it can't override it."** Then explain why: overriding relies on the object's actual runtime type, resolved through a vtable at runtime. Static methods belong to the class, not to any instance, so there's no object to look the runtime type up on — the compiler resolves the call using the **reference type** at compile time instead.

That one sentence — "resolved by reference type, not object type" — is the phrase interviewers are listening for.

slides.sectionTitle: Code: a static "override" that resolves by reference type
Diagram: static dispatch vs dynamic dispatch
slides.markdown:
![Static dispatch versus dynamic dispatch](assets/static-vs-dynamic-dispatch.svg)

Static dispatch is decided once, at compile time, purely from the declared type. Dynamic dispatch is decided fresh on every call, by following the actual object's vtable — which is exactly the mechanism static methods opt out of.

| | Method hiding (static) | Method overriding (instance) |
|---|---|---|
| Resolved | At compile time, by reference type | At runtime, via the object's vtable |
| Requires | Same signature on a static method in the subclass | `@Override` on an instance method with the same signature |
| Calling via a supertype reference | Runs the supertype's version | Runs the subtype's (actual object's) version |
| Polymorphism? | No — no runtime dispatch happens | Yes — this is the mechanism polymorphism relies on |

**How to decide which term applies:** if removing `static` from both methods would change the printed output, you were looking at hiding, not overriding.

slides.sectionTitle: Follow-up: what actually happens if you try?
slides.markdown:
Nothing breaks — the code compiles and runs fine, which is exactly what makes this a trap. What happens is **method hiding**: the subclass's static method with the same signature simply shadows the parent's when called through the subclass type or the subclass instance directly, but a call through a parent-typed reference always resolves to the parent's version, regardless of what object is actually stored there.

No polymorphism occurs at any point — the JVM never consults the object's actual runtime type for a static call.

slides.sectionTitle: Follow-up: does this apply to other languages?
slides.markdown:
Not the same way. Python and JavaScript don't enforce a compile-time static/instance distinction the way Java and C# do — a Python `@staticmethod` can be shadowed on a subclass and accessed through `self`, but Python's dynamic attribute lookup means the behavior looks more like normal attribute resolution than Java's rigid reference-type binding.

The underlying lesson still generalizes — languages with a real compile-time type system tend to bind static calls early; languages without one resolve almost everything dynamically. Naming this contrast is a good way to show breadth without overclaiming the Java rule is universal.

slides.sectionTitle: Follow-up: a static method called through an instance reference — which runs?
slides.markdown:
Calling a static method through an instance (`dogInstance.identify()` instead of `Dog.identify()`) is legal but discouraged — and it still resolves by the **declared type of the reference**, not the runtime object, exactly like the field example. If `dogInstance` is declared as `Animal`, you get `Animal`'s static method even though the object is actually a `Dog`.

The instance is a red herring here: static calls never dispatch on the object at all, whether you write them through a class name or an instance variable.

slides.sectionTitle: Weak answer: saying "no" with no explanation
slides.markdown:
**Weak answer:** "No, you can't override static methods."

**Why it loses points:** it's technically true but empty — it doesn't show you understand *why*, and it invites an immediate, harder follow-up ("then what happens if I try?") that a candidate who only memorized the word "no" can't answer.

**Correct model:** always pair the "no" with the mechanism — static dispatch by reference type at compile time versus dynamic dispatch by object type at runtime — so the follow-up has nothing left to expose.

slides.sectionTitle: Wrong answer: claiming runtime polymorphic dispatch
slides.markdown:
**Wrong answer:** "Yes, if a subclass defines a static method with the same signature, calling it through a supertype reference will run the subclass's version at runtime, just like overriding."

**Why it's wrong:** this is precisely backwards — a call through a supertype-typed reference resolves to the *supertype's* static method, decided at compile time, regardless of the object's actual runtime type. Claiming otherwise means you've confused method hiding with real polymorphic dispatch.

**Correct model:** the reference's declared type decides which static method runs — the object underneath is irrelevant.

"No — you can't override a static method, only hide it. Overriding relies on the object's actual runtime type via a vtable; static methods belong to the class, not an instance, so there's no runtime dispatch to do. `Animal a = new Dog(); a.identify();` calls `Animal`'s static method because the call is resolved by the reference's declared type at compile time, not the object underneath. This is Java/C#-specific — dynamic languages like Python don't draw this same line."
